item.title: Chart of the Week: Jim Jordan overcomes leadership PAC gap
item.description: <p>On Tuesday, House Republicans elected Rep. Jim Jordan (Ohio) to be minority leader in the next Congress. Jordan, currently chairman&hellip;</p>
item.content_encoded:
On Tuesday, House Republicans elected Rep. Jim Jordan (Ohio) to be minority leader in the next Congress. Jordan, currently chairman of the Judiciary Committee, beat out the current No. 2, Majority Leader Steve Scalise (La.).

Both lawmakers had active leadership PACs during this cycle. Politicians use those political action committees to build support for future leadership bids by raising money for other candidates.

Scalise has been far more prolific on that front, using his Eye of the Tiger PAC to distribute $9.7 million to fellow Republicans since 2010, including $1.4 million this cycle.

But Republicans looked past the money and picked Jordan, who has only given out $1.7 million over the same time period from three leadership PACs – with 66% going out during the 2026 cycle.

item.title: Lobbying spending hits Q3 high, remains on pace for another record year
item.description: <p>Lobbying spending approached $1.3 billion in the third quarter of 2026, the highest third-quarter total since Congress began requiring quarterly&hellip;</p>
item.content_encoded:
(Photo by Douglas Rissing/Getty Images)

Lobbying spending approached $1.3 billion in the third quarter of 2026, the highest third-quarter total since Congress began requiring quarterly lobbying reports in 2008.

Federal lobbying spending totaled nearly $4.1 billion through the first nine months of the year, according to an OpenSecrets analysis of federal lobbying disclosures, keeping 2026 on pace to extend a record-setting streak that has seen an annual spending increase every year since 2016. The third-quarter total was up 2.1% — or, about $26.8 million — from the same period in 2025, but represents a 1.8% drop when adjusted for inflation.

Trade associations and the pharmaceutical and manufacturing industries continued to lead the record total of 18,165 organizations that have spent on federal lobbying during the first nine months of the year. The National Association of Realtors — which increased its quarterly lobbying spending by nearly 150% from the same period in 2025 — and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce continued to top the list of individual spenders.

Top firms

Several of the quarter’s leading lobbying firms share a prominent common denominator: strong ties to President Donald Trump’s administration.

Ballard Partners posted a record $34.9 million in third-quarter lobbying revenue — up 5.8% ($1.9 million) from the previous quarter and 39.7% from the same period in 2025.

Ballard reported an unprecedented $98.1 million in lobbying revenue through three quarters. Not only is it the highest total ever recorded by any firm through nine months, but it also surpasses the previous record for a full year — a mark Ballard set in 2025 with $88.1 million — in just nine months.

The firm opened its first Washington office in 2017. Founder Brian Ballard chaired the Trump Victory PAC in 2016 and 2017. Its roster of past employees include former White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, who was replaced days after the midterm elections, and former Attorney General Pam Bondi.

Ballard has reported 399 clients through the first nine months of 2026, and the top six account for 8.96% of its reported compensation. Its top client remained the Puerto Rican bank Bancrédito International Bank & Trust, which paid Ballard $1.9 million. That bank is in liquidation after founder Julio Herrera Veluntini was implicated in a corruption and campaign finance case. Veluntini was pardoned in January 2026 for bribery-related charges after donating $3.5 million to Trump’s super PAC.

Other top clients include Neoprime Capital Partners ($1.6 million), Neobreeze Ltd ($1.5 million) and Tiger Biosciences ($1.4 million).

BGR Group reported $22.5 million in lobbying revenue during the quarter, up 3.3% from the second quarter and 17.4% from the third quarter in 2025. It is led by former Trump campaign adviser David Urban and previously employed Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. BGR Group has raked in $65.2 million across the first three quarters of 2026, and its 388 clients mark a 19.8% increase from 2025.

Miller Strategies reported $18.9 million in quarterly revenue — up $1.7 million (9.8%) from the second quarter — and has pulled in $51.3 million through nine months of 2026. Founder Jeff Miller, a prominent Republican fundraiser appointed by Trump to chair the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Council, was the finance chair for the 2025 presidential inaugural committee. The firm’s record total of 196 clients in 2026 is up 13.3% from last year.

Top spenders

The National Association of Realtors topped all clients by spending $27.4 million in the third quarter, an 87% increase from the second quarter of 2026 and a 149.7% jump from the same period in 2025. The group has spent $57.6 million through nine months of the year, outspending the U.S. Chamber of Commerce by $3 million. The Chamber, the second-leading spender for the year, is the only other organization to top $10 million during the quarter.

The Chamber’s $16.9 million third-quarter outlay marked a 2.8% dip from the second quarter, when it spent $17.4 million, but represented a nearly 20% increase over the $14.1 million it reported in the third quarter in 2025. The business association’s year-to-date spending stands at $54.6 million.

The Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America, the trade group representing branded drugmakers, spent $7.1 million during the quarter. While that marked a 4.3% drop and its second consecutive quarterly decline of 2026, PhRMA remains the third-leading spender overall this year at $26.9 million.

Meanwhile, Koch Inc. posted one of the quarter’s most notable surges, spending $6.9 million on federal lobbying — a 141% increase over its second-quarter output ($2.8 million). It shattered its previous quarterly record of $4.6 million set in the first quarter of 2019 by 48%. The company’s filings reference more than a dozen bills and resolutions, including those addressing excise taxes on major oil and gas companies and Environmental Protection Agency regulations along with legislation related to farming and infrastructure.

Top sectors

Lobbying spending across six  sectors increased compared to the third quarter of 2025, with the largest jumps coming in the construction sector (9.9%), the finance, insurance and real estate sector (9.7%) and the lawyers and lobbyists sector (8.1%). A steady increase also was observed in the communications and electronics sector, which poured in $172 million during the third quarter of 2026 compared to $168 million in the same time period in 2025.

The sharpest decreases came from the ideological and single-issue sectors, which dropped by 10.5% compared with the same period in 2025, and agribusiness, which fell by 6.8%. Spenders classified as “other” fell by 10.3%.

Top issues and bills

Continuing a trend from the first two quarters of 2026, federal spending was the most heavily lobbied issue area, followed by defense, health, taxation and trade. A total of 4,107 clients reported lobbying on budget and appropriations during the third quarter of 2026, while 2,121 lobbied on health issues, 2,227 on defense and 1,692 on tax issues. Lobbying disclosure reports do not break down expenditures by bill or issue, so client counts remain one of the only ways to measure intensity.

The five bills most heavily lobbied in the second quarter were also lobbied most frequently during the third, though in most cases, there were fewer clients lobbying them:

  • The One Big Beautiful Bill remained the most-lobbied piece of legislation, but its number of clients dropped from 767 to 667. Though the bill passed last year, companies and organizations continue to lobby federal agencies over its implementation.
  • The Farm, Food, and National Security Act of 2026, which would reauthorize federal farm policy and nutrition assistance, continued to hold the second spot with 260 clients, down from 287.
  • Lobbying on the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act dropped to 155 clients from 201. The broad bipartisan package aims to expand housing supply by allowing more Community Development Block Grant funding to be used for housing construction, easing regulatory barriers and restricting institutional acquisitions of single-family homes. 
  • The SPEED Act, which would accelerate environmental reviews and fast-track energy and infrastructure projects, ranked fourth with 148 clients, down from 162.
  • Lobbying on the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act, the top legislative priority for the cryptocurrency industry, rose to 138 clients, up from 128 in the second quarter. Despite the lobbying push, the bill failed in a Senate procedural vote in September and is now viewed as unlikely to pass. 

The African Growth and Opportunity Act Extension Act ranked next in number of clients, overtaking two major bills – the Consolidated Appropriations Act (which funded much of the federal government for fiscal 2026) and the National Defense Authorization Act. The AGOA Extension Act, passed by both chambers in September, renewed an agreement that provides eligible African countries with duty-free access to the U.S. market. 

Rounding out the top 10 most-lobbied bills were the Improving Seniors’ Timely Access to Care Act of 2025 – a bill to amend authorization processes under Medicare Advantage – and the Fix Our Forests Act. That legislation has divided environmental advocacy groups, driving lobbying on the bill as it approaches a final vote.

item.title: Voters in several states deliver wins for ballot measures fighting money in politics
item.description: <p>On Election Day, voters not only chose candidates to represent them, but also decided on statewide ballot measures – taking&hellip;</p>
item.content_encoded:
In addition to selecting federal and state officials, Alaskans voted on a ballot measure that would eliminate a requirement that political entities disclosure the “true source” of their funds. (Photo by Christian Moorman/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images)

On Election Day, voters not only chose candidates to represent them, but also decided on statewide ballot measures – taking direct action on matters of policy. 

A total of 164 statewide initiatives appeared on ballots across 40 states in 2026, and seven measures allowed voters to decide directly on laws surrounding money in politics. 

Voters handed major victories to campaign finance reform advocates in Montana and Michigan, and while it remained too close to call as of Nov. 6, Alaska voters appear to have rejected an attempt to undo the state’s anti-dark money law. 

The Institute for Free Speech has already launched federal lawsuits in Montana and Michigan alleging the measures violate free speech rights under the First Amendment.

Here is a closer look at the 2026 ballot measures related to money in politics and how voters decided them:

Voters adopt ‘The Montana Plan’ to ban dark money, corporate political spending

Montana voters approved Initiative 194, referred to as “The Montana Plan,” implementing a new tactic to eliminate dark money and corporate political spending. With 94% of precincts reporting, the vote was 65% in favor to 35% opposed.

The initiative prohibits “artificial persons” such as corporations, nonprofits, trade associations and other entities doing business in Montana from contributing from their general treasuries to candidate campaigns, ballot measures, or political parties. Violations of the initiative would result in forfeiting privileges to do business in the state. 

Political committees, such as political action committees and super PACs, may still raise and spend money donated by individuals.

The Montana Plan support committee raised $1.5 million, including $722,300 from Samantha Walton, the wife of Walmart heir Lukas Walton.

The committee opposing the initiative, Montanans for Free Speech, raised $52,550 from the Montana Chamber of Commerce and the Montana Mining Association. Those groups challenged the initiative’s constitutionality in the state Supreme Court earlier this year, but the court dismissed the case arguing that precedent dictates the court should not rule on the constitutionality of an initiative before it has qualified for the ballot.

The Institute for Free Speech filed a lawsuit Tuesday in the U.S. District Court for the District of Montana on behalf of Frontier Institute, Frontier Action Fund, Montana Family Foundation and the Montana Republican State Central Committee. The plaintiffs allege that the initiative violates their First and 14th Amendment rights.

Supporters argue that since the state has authority to determine what powers corporations possess, it can decide that political spending is not one of them. On its website, the support campaign said that in order to strike the initiative down, “a court would have to say that corporations possess a constitutional entitlement to political-spending power that exists independently of state law. No court has ever said that.”

Alaska voters weigh whether to repeal an anti-dark-money law

Alaskans voted on Ballot Measure 2, which would repeal the state’s top-four primary and ranked-choice voting systems, as well as eliminate a campaign finance provision adopted by voters in 2020 that requires entities to disclose the true source of funds behind their political contributions. 

As of Nov. 6, the measure was still too close to call: 48% in favor and 52% opposed, with 73% of precincts reporting. 

The committee supporting the initiative, Repeal Now, raised $2.8 million, with nearly all of the funding coming from Aurora Action Network, a Wisconsin-based super PAC. Aurora Action Network’s reports disclosing the true source of the group’s funds show contributions from July of $1.5 million from Elon Musk and $675,000 from Pennsylvania billionaire Jeff Yass – two of the three biggest donors to federal political committees this cycle. 

The Opposing committee, No on 2, raised $10.5 million, with $5.3 million from Unite America PAC. The true sources of Unite America’s funds include billionaires Michael Bloomberg, Kathryn Murdoch, and John Arnold, as well as Elon Musk’s brother, Kimbal Musk. (Disclosure: OpenSecrets receives funding from John Arnold’s philanthropic organization, Arnold Ventures.) These contributions were made to Unite America in 2024. Under Alaska’s true source law, an organization that contributes more than $500 to a ballot measure committee is required to file reports disclosing the true source of its funds. If a group makes contributions to a ballot measure committee from its general account (and not a separate account set up for the purpose of making ballot measure committee contributions), it must disclose all contributors to its general account from the preceding 24 months. 

Additionally, on Aug. 18, voters approved Ballot Measure 1 to create campaign contribution limits. Since 2021, campaign contributions in Alaska have been unlimited after its previous limits – established in 2006 – were overturned. 

Under Ballot Measure 1, individuals can donate up to $2,000 each election cycle to a candidate or to a non-group entity influencing the election of a candidate, as well as $5,000 per year to a political party or other group. Organizations that are not political parties can contribute up to $4,000 per election cycle to a candidate and up to $5,000 per year to another group, entity, or political party. Contributions to a joint campaign for governor and lieutenant governor are limited to $4,000 each election cycle for individuals and $8,000 for groups. 

The contribution limits are set to be adjusted for inflation every 10 years beginning in 2031.

Michigan voters ban political spending by some utilities

Michigan voters overwhelmingly approved Proposal 2 – 81% in favor with 95% of precincts reporting. 

The initiative prohibits campaign contributions from certain regulated electric and gas utilities and government contractors that have $250,000 or more in annual government contracts. People and organizations affiliated with such utilities or government contractors – such as a person who holds more than 50% ownership in the company, an executive, a board member, or their family members – would also be prohibited from making campaign contributions. 

Additionally, Proposal 2 expanded the definition of “expenditure” to include communications that promote, support, attack, or oppose a candidate or ballot measure, even when that communication is made without express advocacy. It also requires disclosure when a group spends $5,000 or more on political ads within 100 days of a general election or 30 days of a primary election and applies disclosure requirements to political ads on the internet and digital platforms. 

Michiganders for Money Out of Politics raised $10.3 million with support from All Hands on Deck Network, Pro-Democracy Campaign, Sixteen Thirty Fund, Michigan United, and Green Advocacy Project. 

The opposition committee, Protect MI Free Speech, raised $579,000. Contributors included the Michigan Infrastructure and Transportation Association, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan, CMS Energy Corporation and Comcast Financial Agency Corp. 

The Institute for Free Speech filed a lawsuit Tuesday in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Michigan on behalf of Mackinac Center for Public Policy, a conservative think tank. Similar to the lawsuit challenging the Montana Plan, plaintiffs allege that the initiative violates their First and 14th Amendment rights.

California voters consider whether to repeal a ban on public campaign financing

Proposition 4, which would repeal the state’s ban on public campaign financing, remained too close to call as of Nov. 6 with 51% of voters opposed and 68% of the vote counted.

The measure was referred to the ballot by the California Legislature last year with all Democratic lawmakers voting in favor and all Republicans voting against.

The committees supporting the measure — Californians for Fair Elections and Movement Voter PAC Supporting Prop 4 — raised $984,582 through Oct. 17, with the California Nurses Association donating $250,000 to Californians for Fair Elections on Oct. 2.

Supporters pointed to 14 states and the District of Columbia that provide for public campaign financing for certain offices. In voicing its opposition to the measure, the California Taxpayers Association argued that public money should not fund elections.

No committee formed to oppose the measure.

Arizona rejects ban on foreign election spending

Voters in Arizona rejected Proposition 144, a constitutional amendment that would have banned foreign nationals from contributing money to influence the state’s elections. 

The amendment contained several other provisions. It would have provided that “only citizens may register and vote in Arizona elections,” required government-issued ID to vote, created a constitutional requirement that voters may have their vote tabulated at their voting location on Election Day and lowered the legal standard for judicial review of election laws.

The amendment was placed on the ballot by the Arizona Legislature with all Republican legislators in favor and all Democrats opposed.

As of Nov. 6, 53% of voters said no to Proposition 144, according to the Arizona Secretary of State’s office.

A similar measure in Missouri that would have, in part, banned foreign nationals and foreign adversaries from spending on ballot measures was overwhelmingly rejected during the state’s August primary.

Michigan voters ban political spending by some utilities

Michigan voters overwhelmingly approved Proposal 2 – 81% in favor with 95% of precincts reporting. 

The initiative prohibits campaign contributions from certain regulated electric and gas utilities and government contractors that have $250,000 or more in annual government contracts. People and organizations affiliated with such utilities or government contractors – such as a person who holds more than 50% ownership in the company, an executive, a board member, or their family members – would also be prohibited from making campaign contributions. 

Additionally, Proposal 2 expanded the definition of “expenditure” to include communications that promote, support, attack, or oppose a candidate or ballot measure, even when that communication is made without express advocacy. It also requires disclosure when a group spends $5,000 or more on political ads within 100 days of a general election or 30 days of a primary election and applies disclosure requirements to political ads on the internet and digital platforms. 

Michiganders for Money Out of Politics raised $10.3 million with support from All Hands on Deck Network, Pro-Democracy Campaign, Sixteen Thirty Fund, Michigan United, and Green Advocacy Project. 

The opposition committee, Protect MI Free Speech, raised $579,000. Contributors included the Michigan Infrastructure and Transportation Association, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan, CMS Energy Corporation and Comcast Financial Agency Corp. 

The Institute for Free Speech filed a lawsuit Tuesday in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Michigan on behalf of Mackinac Center for Public Policy, a conservative think tank. Similar to the lawsuit challenging the Montana Plan, plaintiffs allege that the initiative violates their First and 14th Amendment rights.

California voters consider whether to repeal a ban on public campaign financing

Proposition 4, which would repeal the state’s ban on public campaign financing, remained too close to call as of Nov. 6 with 51% of voters opposed and 68% of the vote counted.

The measure was referred to the ballot by the California Legislature last year with all Democratic lawmakers voting in favor and all Republicans voting against.

The committees supporting the measure — Californians for Fair Elections and Movement Voter PAC Supporting Prop 4 — raised $984,582 through Oct. 17, with the California Nurses Association donating $250,000 to Californians for Fair Elections on Oct. 2.

Supporters pointed to 14 states and the District of Columbia that provide for public campaign financing for certain offices. In voicing its opposition to the measure, the California Taxpayers Association argued that public money should not fund elections.

No committee formed to oppose the measure.

Arizona rejects ban on foreign election spending

Voters in Arizona rejected Proposition 144, a constitutional amendment that would have banned foreign nationals from contributing money to influence the state’s elections. 

The amendment contained several other provisions. It would have provided that “only citizens may register and vote in Arizona elections,” required government-issued ID to vote, created a constitutional requirement that voters may have their vote tabulated at their voting location on Election Day and lowered the legal standard for judicial review of election laws.

The amendment was placed on the ballot by the Arizona Legislature with all Republican legislators in favor and all Democrats opposed.

As of Nov. 6, 53% of voters said no to Proposition 144, according to the Arizona Secretary of State’s office.

A similar measure in Missouri that would have, in part, banned foreign nationals and foreign adversaries from spending on ballot measures was overwhelmingly rejected during the state’s August primary.
